def stream_for_type(physical_type: jelly.PhysicalStreamType) -> type[Stream]:
    """
    Give a Stream based on physical type specified.

    Args:
        physical_type (jelly.PhysicalStreamType): jelly stream physical type.

    Raises:
        NotImplementedError: if no stream for requested physical type is available.

    Returns:
        type[Stream]: jelly stream

    """
    try:
        stream_cls = STREAM_DISPATCH[physical_type]
    except KeyError:
        if physical_type == jelly.PHYSICAL_STREAM_TYPE_GRAPHS:
            msg = (
                "writing streams of the GRAPHS physical type is not supported "
                "(they can still be read). Use QUADS instead."
            )
        else:
            msg = (
                "no stream class for physical type "
                f"{jelly.PhysicalStreamType.Name(physical_type)}"
            )
        raise NotImplementedError(msg) from None
    return stream_cls

docs.title: Generic API
docs.text: This guide explains how to use pyjelly’s generic API to write and read RDF statements into the Jelly format without any external library.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install pyjelly from PyPI:

pip install pyjelly

The requirements are the same as with RDFLib.

docs.title: Usage without external libraries
docs.text: Unlike the example in getting started, the Generic API does not use the RDFLib or any other third-party libraries, but it works in much the same way.

docs.title: Serializing statements to a Jelly file
docs.text:
To make a set of triples/quads and write them to a Jelly file, use:

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import *

# Create a generic sink object
generic_sink = GenericStatementSink()

# Let's add triples one by one
generic_sink.add(
    Triple(
        IRI("http://example.com/subject"),
        IRI("http://example.com/predicate"),
        Literal("Hello", langtag="en"),
    )
)
generic_sink.add(
    Triple(
        BlankNode("B1"),
        IRI("http://example.com/hasName"),
        Literal("Bob"),
    )
)

# Write into a Jelly file
with open("output.jelly", "wb") as out_file:
    generic_sink.serialize(out_file)

print("All done.")

This example uses pyjelly’s simple custom triple/quad type, which is easy to create and work with.

The terms in the statements are IRI, BlankNode and Literal. You can read their parts with IRI.iri, BlankNode.identifier, and Literal.lex, Literal.langtag, Literal.datatype (the datatype IRI as a string) and Literal.direction. str() gives a term in N-Triples syntax, e.g., <http://example.com/subject> or "Hello"@en.

docs.title: Parsing statements from a Jelly file
docs.text:
To load triples/quads from a .jelly file into a GenericStatementSink, see:

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import *

# Create a generic sink object
generic_sink = GenericStatementSink()

# Load triples from the Jelly file
with open("output.jelly", "rb") as in_file:
    generic_sink.parse(in_file)

# Let's inspect them statement by statement
for statement in generic_sink:
    if isinstance(statement, Triple):
        print(statement)

print("All done.")

GenericStatementSink keeps all statements in memory. To read a large file statement by statement instead, use parse_jelly_flat in a generator:

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.parse import parse_jelly_flat


# Helper generator that streams statements from a Jelly file path
def stream_statements(jelly_path):
    with open(jelly_path, "rb") as f:
        # Statements are read one by one, as they are needed
        yield from parse_jelly_flat(f)


# Example usage, just printing:
for statement in stream_statements("output.jelly"):
    print(statement)

print("All done.")

Only the statement that is being processed is kept in memory.

docs.title: Parsing a stream of graphs
docs.text:
Similarly, to process a Jelly stream as a stream of graphs through generic API, see:

import gzip
import urllib.request
from itertools import islice

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.parse import parse_jelly_grouped

# Dataset: Katrina weather measurements (10k graphs)
# Documentation: https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/lod-katrina/dev
url = "https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/lod-katrina/dev/files/jelly_10K.jelly.gz"

# Load, uncompress .gz file, and pass to Jelly parser, all in a streaming manner
with (
    urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response,
    gzip.open(response) as jelly_stream,
):
    # Parse into sinks (one per graph)
    graphs = parse_jelly_grouped(jelly_stream)

    # Only the first 50 graphs, the rest will not be parsed
    for i, graph in enumerate(islice(graphs, 50)):
        print(f"Graph {i} in the stream has {len(graph)} triples")

We use a dataset of weather measurements and count the number of triples in each graph.

docs.title: Parsing a stream of statements
docs.text:
You can also process a Jelly stream as a flat stream of statements. We look through a fragment of Denmark's OpenStreetMap to find all city names:

import gzip
import urllib.request

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import *
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.parse import parse_jelly_flat

# Dataset: OpenStreetMap data for Denmark (first 10k objects)
# Documentation: https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/osm2rdf-denmark/dev
url = (
    "https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/osm2rdf-denmark/dev/files/jelly_10K.jelly.gz"
)

# We are looking for city names in the dataset
predicate_to_look_for = IRI("https://www.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:addr:city")
city_names = set()

with (
    urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response,
    gzip.open(response) as jelly_stream,
):
    for event in parse_jelly_flat(jelly_stream):
        if isinstance(event, Triple):  # we are only interested in triples
            if event.p == predicate_to_look_for:
                city_names.add(event.o.lex)

print(f"Found {len(city_names)} unique city names in the dataset.")
print("Sample city names:")
for city in list(city_names)[:10]:
    print(f"- {city}")

parse_jelly_flat returns a generator of statements, so the file is processed statement by statement.

docs.title: Serializing a stream of graphs
docs.text:
If you have a generator object containing graphs, you can use a generic approach for serialization:

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import *
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.serialize import grouped_stream_to_file
import random


# Example generator that yields graphs
def generate_sample_sinks():
    for _ in range(10):
        sink = GenericStatementSink()
        sink.add(
            Triple(
                IRI("http://example.com/sensor"),
                IRI("http://example.com/humidity"),
                Literal(str(random.random())),
            )
        )
        yield sink


output_file = "output.jelly"
print(f"Streaming graphs into {output_file}…")
with open(output_file, "wb") as out_f:
    grouped_stream_to_file(generate_sample_sinks(), out_f)
print("All done.")

Each sink is written as one RDF Message, so the grouping is kept when the stream is read with parse_jelly_grouped.

docs.title: Serializing a stream of statements
docs.text:
If you have a generator object containing statements, you can serialize it like this:

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.serialize import flat_stream_to_file
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import *
import random


# Example generator that yields raw triples
def generate_sample_triples():
    for _ in range(10):
        yield Triple(
            IRI("http://example.com/sensor"),
            IRI("http://example.com/humidity"),
            Literal(str(random.random())),
        )


output_file = "flat_output.jelly"
print(f"Streaming triples into {output_file}…")
sample_triples = generate_sample_triples()
with open(output_file, "wb") as out_f:
    flat_stream_to_file(sample_triples, out_f)
print("All done.")

The statements are written in order, as one flat stream.

docs.title: Working with byte buffers and Kafka
docs.text:
When working with Kafka or other message brokers, you may want to write Jelly data to a byte buffer instead of a file. You can do this by using the BytesIO class from the io module:

import io

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import *

g1 = GenericStatementSink()

g1.add(
    Triple(
        IRI("http://example.com/subject"),
        IRI("http://example.com/predicate"),
        Literal("Hello", langtag="en"),
    )
)

# Write the data into a byte buffer (bytes type)
with io.BytesIO() as write_buffer:
    g1.serialize(write_buffer)
    data = write_buffer.getvalue()

print(f"Serialized data size: {len(data)} bytes")

# Parse the data back
g2 = GenericStatementSink()
with io.BytesIO(data) as read_buffer:
    g2.parse(read_buffer)

print("\nParsed triples:")
for statement in g2:
    print(statement)

The data variable is of type bytes, and can be passed to Kafka with KafkaProducer.send(value=data), or any other API that accepts byte buffers. With the RDFLib integration, write to the buffer with graph.serialize(destination=buffer, format="jelly"), and read the bytes back with graph.parse(data=data, format="jelly").

When working with Kafka, you should be aware of the broker's offset management and partitioning strategies. Data within one Jelly stream must be strictly ordered and no frames may be dropped. If you have less strict ordering guarantees, you should split up the stream into multiple Jelly streams, each with guaranteed consistency.

docs.title: Accessing stream frame metadata
docs.text:
It is possible to access RdfStreamFrame metadata in pyjelly via context variables. To do that, define a context variable before parsing and pass it as argument to parser functions, e.g.:

from collections.abc import MutableMapping
from contextvars import ContextVar
import urllib.request

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.parse import parse_jelly_grouped

frame_metadata: ContextVar[MutableMapping[str, bytes]] = ContextVar("frame_metadata")

url = "https://registry.petapico.org/nanopubs.jelly"
with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response:
    graphs = parse_jelly_grouped(response, frame_metadata=frame_metadata)
    # Just show the first graph
    graph = next(graphs)
    print(f"The first graph in the stream has {len(graph)} triples.")
    print(f"Its frame metadata: {frame_metadata.get()}")

docs.title: See also
docs.text: If you are familiar with RDFLib, you can use pyjelly together with RDFLib in a similar way. See the dedicated guide.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This guide walks you through installing and working with pyjelly and RDFLib.

docs.title: Installation (with RDFLib)
docs.text:
Install pyjelly from PyPI:

pip install pyjelly[rdflib]

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer
  • Linux, macOS, or Windows

docs.title: Usage with RDFLib
docs.text: Once you install pyjelly, it integrates automatically with RDFLib through standard RDFLib API.

docs.title: Serializing a graph
docs.text:
To serialize a graph to the Jelly format see:

from rdflib import Graph

g = Graph()
g.parse("https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-ssn/integrated/examples/sunspots.ttl")
g.serialize(destination="sunspots.jelly", format="jelly")
print(f"Wrote {len(g)} triples to sunspots.jelly")

This creates a delimited Jelly stream using default options.

docs.title: Including namespace declarations (prefixes)
docs.text:
By default, Jelly serializes only triples/quads. To also include namespace declarations (prefixes) in the output, enable the namespace_declarations option. Prefixes bound in RDFLib's namespace manager will then be written into the Jelly stream and restored on parsing.

from rdflib import Graph, Literal, Namespace
from rdflib.namespace import FOAF

from pyjelly.options import StreamParameters
from pyjelly.serialize.streams import SerializerOptions

# Build a tiny graph and bind a prefix
EX = Namespace("http://example.org/")
g = Graph()
g.bind("ex", EX)
g.add((EX.alice, FOAF.name, Literal("Alice")))

# Enable namespace declarations in Jelly output
options = SerializerOptions(params=StreamParameters(namespace_declarations=True))
g.serialize("namespaces.jelly", format="jelly", options=options)

# Parse back and check that the prefix is there
g_new = Graph()
g_new.parse("namespaces.jelly", format="jelly")
print("Prefix ex:", dict(g_new.namespaces()).get("ex"))

Tip

For an existing graph you can (re)bind a prefix just before saving:

g.namespace_manager.bind("ex", EX, replace=True)

RDFLib binds about 30 common prefixes to every new graph, and they are all written as well. To write only the prefixes you bind yourself, create the graph with Graph(bind_namespaces="none").

docs.title: Parsing a graph
docs.text:
To load RDF data from a .jelly file see:

from rdflib import Graph

g = Graph()
g.parse("sunspots.jelly", format="jelly")

print("Parsed triples:")
for s, p, o in g:
    print(f"{s} {p} {o}")

RDFLib will reconstruct the graph from the Jelly file.

docs.title: Parsing a stream of graphs
docs.text:
You can process a Jelly stream as a stream of graphs. A Jelly stream can hold a sequence of graphs, each in its own RDF Message – we can load each one as a separate RDFLib graph.

In this example, we use a dataset of weather measurements. We count the number of triples in each graph:

import gzip
import urllib.request
from itertools import islice

from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.parse import parse_jelly_grouped

# Dataset: Katrina weather measurements (10k graphs)
# Documentation: https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/lod-katrina/dev
url = "https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/lod-katrina/dev/files/jelly_10K.jelly.gz"

# Load, uncompress .gz file, and pass to Jelly parser, all in a streaming manner
with (
    urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response,
    gzip.open(response) as jelly_stream,
):
    graphs = parse_jelly_grouped(jelly_stream)
    # Only the first 50 graphs, the rest will not be parsed
    for i, graph in enumerate(islice(graphs, 50)):
        print(f"Graph {i} in the stream has {len(graph)} triples")

Each iteration receives only one graph, allowing for processing large datasets efficiently, without exhausting memory.

docs.title: Parsing a stream of triples
docs.text:
You can also process a Jelly stream as a flat stream of triples.

We look through a fragment of Denmark's OpenStreetMap to find all city names:

import gzip
import urllib.request

from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.parse import parse_jelly_flat
from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.statements import Triple
from rdflib import URIRef

# Dataset: OpenStreetMap data for Denmark (first 10k objects)
# Documentation: https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/osm2rdf-denmark/dev
url = (
    "https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/osm2rdf-denmark/dev/files/jelly_10K.jelly.gz"
)

# We are looking for city names in the dataset
predicate_to_look_for = URIRef("https://www.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:addr:city")
city_names = set()

with (
    urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response,
    gzip.open(response) as jelly_stream,
):
    for event in parse_jelly_flat(jelly_stream):
        if isinstance(event, Triple):  # we are only interested in triples
            if event.p == predicate_to_look_for:
                city_names.add(event.o)

print(f"Found {len(city_names)} unique city names in the dataset.")
print("Sample city names:")
for city in list(city_names)[:10]:
    print(f"- {city}")

parse_jelly_flat returns a generator of stream events (i.e., statements parsed). This case allows you to efficiently process the file triple-by-triple and build custom aggregations from the stream.

docs.title: Checking IRIs
docs.text: By default, the IRIs in a Jelly file are not checked when it is read into RDFLib, which makes reading faster. To turn it on, set validate_iris=True, e.g., graph.parse("data.jelly", format="jelly", validate_iris=True). The parsing functions in pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.parse take the same argument.

docs.title: Serializing a stream of graphs
docs.text:
If you have a generator object containing graphs, you can easily serialize it into the Jelly format: 

from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.serialize import grouped_stream_to_file

from rdflib import Graph, Literal, Namespace
import random


def generate_sample_graphs():
    ex = Namespace("http://example.org/")
    for _ in range(10):
        g = Graph()
        g.add((ex.sensor, ex.temperature, Literal(random.random())))
        g.add((ex.sensor, ex.humidity, Literal(random.random())))
        yield g


output_file_name = "output.jelly"

print(f"Streaming graphs into {output_file_name}…")
sample_graphs = generate_sample_graphs()
with open(output_file_name, "wb") as out_file:
    grouped_stream_to_file(sample_graphs, out_file)
print("All done.")

This method allows for transmitting logically grouped data, preserving their original division: each graph is one RDF Message.

docs.title: Serializing a stream of statements
docs.text:
If you have a generator object containing statements, you can easily serialize it into the Jelly format: 

from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.serialize import flat_stream_to_file
from rdflib import Literal, Namespace
import random


# example generator with triples statements
def generate_sample_triples():
    ex = Namespace("http://example.org/")
    for _ in range(10):
        yield (ex.sensor, ex.temperature, Literal(random.random()))


output_file_name = "flat_output.jelly"

print(f"Streaming triples into {output_file_name}…")
sample_triples = generate_sample_triples()
with open(output_file_name, "wb") as out_file:
    flat_stream_to_file(sample_triples, out_file)
print("All done.")

The flat method transmits the data as a continuous sequence of statements, keeping it simple and ordered.

For more control over framing and other options, see pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.serialize in the API reference.

docs.title: File extension support
docs.text:
When parsing, you can generally omit the format="jelly" parameter if the file ends in .jelly – RDFLib will auto-detect the format:

from rdflib import Graph
import pyjelly.integrations.rdflib

g = Graph()
g.parse("sunspots.jelly")
print(f"Parsed {len(g)} triples")

Warning

Unfortunately, the way this is implemented in RDFLib is a bit wonky, so it will only work if you explicitly import pyjelly.integrations.rdflib, or you used format="jelly" in a serialize() or parse() call before.

This only works for parsing. serialize() does not look at the file extension, so g.serialize("out.jelly") writes Turtle. Always pass format="jelly" when serializing.

docs.title: NetworkX
docs.text:
NetworkX is a Python package that represents complex networks as graphs and allows for their manipulation.

Install the following libraries:

pip install pyjelly[rdflib] networkx matplotlib

docs.title: Parse graph, show it
docs.text:
Let's investigate relationships between worldwide political figures (support and opposition relations)! We are given a graph in .jelly containing information about political stances extracted from news articles. Let's dive in and get some useful information!

We can easily load it: 

# Parse RDF from the Jelly format
rdf_g = Graph()
rdf_g.parse(example_file, format="jelly")
print(f"Loaded graph with {len(rdf_g)} triples.")

Output from print():

Loaded graph with 90000 triples.

Convert it into a convenient NetworkX graph:

# Convert to a NetworkX graph
nx_g = rdflib_to_networkx_graph(rdf_g_filtered)

Is our graph fully connected? It's important to know (are all political relations tied together?), let's check here:

# Example calculation, get the number of connected components in a graph
num_components = nx.number_connected_components(nx_g)
print(f"Connected components: {num_components}")

Output from print():

Connected components: 24

Which nodes are connected the most (have most connections?), let's see top 5 of them:

# Example calculation, get top 5 objects with highest degrees, simple in NetworkX
top5 = sorted(nx_g.degree, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:5]
print("Top 5 nodes sorted by degree:")
for node, deg in top5:
    print(f"{node}: {deg}")

Output from print():

Top 5 nodes sorted by degree:
Sócrates: 241
Cavaco: 189
Passos Coelho: 187
Costa: 179
António Costa: 168

What is the shortest path between two nodes? We can check:

# Helper function
norm = lambda n: (
    str(n.value).strip().lower() if isinstance(n, Literal) else str(n).strip().lower()
)

# Example calculation, shortest path between two nodes (provided at least two nodes)
source = next(n for n in nx_g if norm(n) == "socrates")
target = next(n for n in nx_g if norm(n) == "obama")
# There may be several shortest paths, take the first one in alphabetical order
path = min(
    nx.all_shortest_paths(nx_g, source=source, target=target),
    key=lambda p: [str(n) for n in p],
)
print(f"Shortest path from {source} to {target}: {' -> '.join(path)}")

Output from print():

Shortest path from Socrates to Obama: Socrates -> Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa -> António Costa -> Obama

However, it's best to see the full picture (for our example we truncate to 10 nodes for clarity):

# Take first 10 nodes
nodes = list(nx_g)[:10]
subg = nx_g.subgraph(nodes)

# Draw and display the graph
pos_sub = nx.spring_layout(subg, k=5, iterations=200, scale=3, seed=24)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))

# Introduce your own settings for display
nx.draw_networkx(subg, pos_sub, font_size=14, node_size=220, linewidths=0.7)
plt.axis("off")
plt.show()

The graph presents as follows

In summary:

Entire example 
import urllib.request, gzip, tempfile, shutil, os

import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rdflib import Graph, URIRef, BNode, Literal
from rdflib.extras.external_graph_libs import rdflib_to_networkx_graph

# Filter predicates for people
TARGET_PREDICATES = {
    URIRef("http://www.politiquices.pt/ent2_str"),
    URIRef("http://www.politiquices.pt/ent1_str"),
}

# URL to the dataset
url = "https://w3id.org/riverbench/datasets/politiquices/1.0.3/files/jelly_10K.jelly.gz"

# Load example jelly file
with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as r:
    fd, example_file = tempfile.mkstemp(suffix=".jelly")
    os.close(fd)
    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=r) as g, open(example_file, "wb") as out:
        shutil.copyfileobj(g, out)

# Parse RDF from the Jelly format
rdf_g = Graph()
rdf_g.parse(example_file, format="jelly")
print(f"Loaded graph with {len(rdf_g)} triples.")

# First step for filtering the graph
rdf_g_filtered = Graph()
for s, p, o in rdf_g.triples((None, None, None)):
    if p in TARGET_PREDICATES:
        rdf_g_filtered.add((s, p, o))

# Just filtering the graph for clarity of visualization, can be omitted
related = URIRef("http://www.politiquices.pt/related")
for b in list(rdf_g_filtered.subjects()):
    if isinstance(b, BNode):
        ent1 = ent2 = None
        for p, o in rdf_g_filtered.predicate_objects(b):
            if p == URIRef("http://www.politiquices.pt/ent1_str") and isinstance(
                o, Literal
            ):
                ent1 = o
            elif p == URIRef("http://www.politiquices.pt/ent2_str") and isinstance(
                o, Literal
            ):
                ent2 = o
        if ent1 and ent2:
            rdf_g_filtered.add((ent1, related, ent2))
            rdf_g_filtered.add((ent2, related, ent1))
        for triple in list(rdf_g_filtered.triples((b, None, None))):
            rdf_g_filtered.remove(triple)

# Convert to a NetworkX graph
nx_g = rdflib_to_networkx_graph(rdf_g_filtered)

# Example calculation, get the number of connected components in a graph
num_components = nx.number_connected_components(nx_g)
print(f"Connected components: {num_components}")

# Example calculation, get top 5 objects with highest degrees, simple in NetworkX
top5 = sorted(nx_g.degree, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:5]
print("Top 5 nodes sorted by degree:")
for node, deg in top5:
    print(f"{node}: {deg}")

# Helper function
norm = lambda n: (
    str(n.value).strip().lower() if isinstance(n, Literal) else str(n).strip().lower()
)

# Example calculation, shortest path between two nodes (provided at least two nodes)
source = next(n for n in nx_g if norm(n) == "socrates")
target = next(n for n in nx_g if norm(n) == "obama")
# There may be several shortest paths, take the first one in alphabetical order
path = min(
    nx.all_shortest_paths(nx_g, source=source, target=target),
    key=lambda p: [str(n) for n in p],
)
print(f"Shortest path from {source} to {target}: {' -> '.join(path)}")

# Take first 10 nodes
nodes = list(nx_g)[:10]
subg = nx_g.subgraph(nodes)

# Draw and display the graph
pos_sub = nx.spring_layout(subg, k=5, iterations=200, scale=3, seed=24)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))

# Introduce your own settings for display
nx.draw_networkx(subg, pos_sub, font_size=14, node_size=220, linewidths=0.7)
plt.axis("off")
plt.show()

print("All done.")

We converted an RDFLib graph to NetworkX, calculated insightful metrics and visualized the graph.

For more info about the data source please see the Politiquices dataset in RiverBench and its original source (Portuguese).

docs.title: Serialize NetworkX graph
docs.text:
This example shows how to write a NetworkX graph to a Jelly file:

import networkx as nx
from rdflib import Graph, URIRef, Namespace
from rdflib.namespace import RDF

# An example NetworkX graph
nx_g = nx.Graph()
nx_g.add_node("http://example.org/A")
nx_g.add_node("http://example.org/B")
nx_g.add_edge("http://example.org/A", "http://example.org/B")

# We define RDFLib graph for further conversion
rdf_g = Graph()

# Example namespace
ex = Namespace("http://example.org/ns#")

# Add triples through node information in NetworkX graph
for node_uri, data in nx_g.nodes(data=True):
    subj = URIRef(node_uri)
    rdf_g.add((subj, RDF.type, ex.Node))

# Add triples through edge information in NetworkX graph
for u, v, attr in nx_g.edges(data=True):
    rdf_g.add((URIRef(u), ex.connectedTo, URIRef(v)))

# Serialize graph into a .jelly file
rdf_g.serialize(destination="networkx_graph.jelly", format="jelly")
print("All done.")

Which converts the NetworkX graph into an RDFLib Graph instance and serializes it.

docs.title: What is Jelly and pyjelly?
docs.text:
Jelly is a high-performance serialization format for RDF knowledge graphs and knowledge graph streams. It's designed to be fast, compact, and flexible.

With Jelly, you can transmit both flat and structured streams of triples, quads, graphs, and datasets. Jelly works well in both batch and real-time settings – including files, sockets, or streaming protocols like Kafka or gRPC.

pyjelly is a Python implementation of the Jelly protocol. It provides:

  • Full support for reading and writing Jelly-encoded RDF data
  • Reading and writing SPARQL query results in Jelly-SPARQL
  • Seamless integration with RDFLib ("works just like Turtle")
  • Standalone generic API that doesn't need RDFLib or any other RDF library
  • Support for all Jelly stream types
  • Tools for working with delimited and non-delimited Jelly streams
  • Fine-grained control over serialization options and framing

docs.title: Jelly-RDF versions
docs.text:
pyjelly reads all versions of Jelly-RDF: 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2. It writes Jelly-RDF 1.2 by default, which is smaller and faster than Jelly-RDF 1.1.

Older Jelly parsers can't read Jelly-RDF 1.2. To write Jelly-RDF 1.1 for them, set the protocol version to 2:

from pyjelly.options import StreamParameters
from pyjelly.serialize.streams import SerializerOptions

options = SerializerOptions(params=StreamParameters(version=2))
graph.serialize("out.jelly", format="jelly", options=options)

docs.title: Supported stream types
docs.text:
pyjelly writes the TRIPLES and QUADS physical stream types. It can also read GRAPHS, which only exists in Jelly-RDF 1.0 and 1.1.

A Jelly-RDF 1.2 stream is either one graph or dataset, or a sequence of RDF Messages. When you write a stream of graphs or datasets (e.g., with grouped_stream_to_file), each is an RDF Message. When you read such a stream with parse_jelly_grouped, you get one graph or dataset per message.

docs.title: RDF 1.2
docs.text:
The generic API supports RDF 1.2: triple terms, as a Triple in the object of a statement, and directional language-tagged strings, as Literal("text", "en", direction="ltr"). RDFLib 7 doesn't support RDF 1.2 yet.

To declare that a stream uses RDF 1.2, set rdf_version=jelly.RDF_VERSION_1_2 in StreamParameters (jelly is pyjelly.jelly). GenericStatementSink.serialize() doesn't take options, so write the statements with flat_stream_to_file or grouped_stream_to_file:

from pyjelly import jelly
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import IRI, Literal, Triple
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.parse import parse_jelly_flat
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.serialize import flat_stream_to_file
from pyjelly.options import StreamParameters
from pyjelly.serialize.streams import SerializerOptions

alice = IRI("http://example.org/alice")


def generate_statements():
    # A triple term in the object of a statement
    yield Triple(
        alice,
        IRI("http://example.org/says"),
        Triple(alice, IRI("http://example.org/knows"), IRI("http://example.org/bob")),
    )
    # A language-tagged string with a base direction
    yield Triple(
        alice, IRI("http://example.org/name"), Literal("Alice", "en", direction="ltr")
    )


# Declare that the stream uses RDF 1.2
options = SerializerOptions(params=StreamParameters(rdf_version=jelly.RDF_VERSION_1_2))
with open("rdf12.jelly", "wb") as out_file:
    flat_stream_to_file(generate_statements(), out_file, options=options)

with open("rdf12.jelly", "rb") as in_file:
    for statement in parse_jelly_flat(in_file):
        print(statement)

docs.title: SPARQL query results
docs.text: pyjelly reads and writes the results of SELECT and ASK queries in Jelly-SPARQL, with RDFLib's Result.parse and Result.serialize, or with the generic API. See SPARQL query results.

docs.title: Conformance to the Jelly specification
docs.text:
pyjelly is continuously tested for conformance to the Jelly specification. It passes the conformance tests of Jelly-RDF 1.2, and the tests of Jelly-RDF 1.1, except for writing the GRAPHS physical stream type. It also passes the conformance tests of Jelly-SPARQL.

See the conformance tests in the pyjelly repository.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Use cases for pyjelly include:

  • Client-server communication – link your client app in Python to the server (e.g., Apache Jena, RDF4J) with Jelly to reduce latency and improve user experience.
  • Inter-service communication – use Jelly to efficiently exchange RDF data between microservices.
  • Data science workflows – use Jelly to read and write RDF data in data science pipelines, enabling efficient processing of large datasets.
    • pyjelly is fully streaming, so it can handle large datasets without loading everything into memory at once.
    • We are working on support for pandas and other data science libraries – stay tuned for updates!
  • Database dumps and bulk loads – quickly read and write large RDF datasets with Jelly, reducing storage space and improving database maintenance tasks.

docs.title: Integrations with other libraries
docs.text:
pyjelly works with libraries that connect to RDFLib, see:

  • RDFLib-Neo4j integration
  • NetworkX integration

docs.title: Pre-compiled binaries
docs.text:
pyjelly is written in pure Python, so you can run it on any platform that supports Python. We also provide pre-compiled binaries using mypyc for better performance. Supported platforms include Windows, macOS, and Linux (x86_64 and ARM64). When installing pyjelly, your package manager will automatically download the right binary, or, if your platform is not supported, it will automatically fall back to the pure Python implementation. You can find the full list of supported platforms on pypi.

In rudimentary benchmarks, the mypyc-compiled version of pyjelly is 20–80% faster than the pure Python version, depending on the workload.

docs.title: RDFLib-Neo4j
docs.text:
Info

This is an integration with Neo4j via the RDFLib-Neo4j library. It works with all Neo4j instances, including AuraDB, but is limited in features and performance. If you are self-hosting Neo4j (Neo4j Desktop or Community/Enterprise), consider using the Jelly-Neo4j plugin for neosemantics, which offers better performance and more features.

RDFLib-Neo4j lets you import RDF triples into Neo4j via the RDFLib API.

Install the following library: 

pip install pyjelly[rdflib] rdflib-neo4j

docs.title: Parsing data from a Jelly file into Neo4j
docs.text:
To parse data from a .jelly file into the Neo4j database, use the following example (insert the URI and credentials of your Neo4j instance, e.g., AuraDB):

Parsing 
import urllib.request
from neo4j import GraphDatabase
from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib_neo4j import Neo4jStoreConfig, Neo4jStore, HANDLE_VOCAB_URI_STRATEGY

# Example file from the Riverbench
example_file, _ = urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://w3id.org/riverbench/v/dev.jelly")

# Please introduce your credentials, e.g., of your AuraDB instance
aura_db_uri = "aura_db_uri"
aura_db_username = "neo4j"
aura_db_pwd = "aura_db_pwd"

# Prepare the authentication data for Neo4j
auth_data = {
    "uri": aura_db_uri,
    "database": "neo4j",
    "user": aura_db_username,
    "pwd": aura_db_pwd,
}

# Prepare the configuration for Neo4jStore object
config = Neo4jStoreConfig(
    auth_data=auth_data,
    handle_vocab_uri_strategy=HANDLE_VOCAB_URI_STRATEGY.IGNORE,
    batching=True,
)

# Make a graph with Neo4jStore object
neo4j_sink = Graph(store=Neo4jStore(config=config))

# Parse the file into Neo4j
neo4j_sink.parse(example_file, format="jelly")

# Close the store, which writes the remaining batch
neo4j_sink.close(True)

# Cypher query to check loaded data
with GraphDatabase.driver(
    aura_db_uri, auth=(aura_db_username, aura_db_pwd)
).session() as session:
    # Triples with literal objects are stored as node properties, not relationships
    count = session.run("MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN count(r) AS c").single()["c"]
    print(f"Loaded {count} relationships")
    for r in session.run(
        "MATCH (s)-[r]->(o) RETURN s.uri AS s, type(r) AS p, o.uri AS o LIMIT 5"
    ):
        print(r["s"], f"-[{r['p']}]->", r["o"])

print("All done.")

which inserts your data into your Neo4j database.

  • Neo4j Labs: RDFLib-Neo4j

docs.title: SPARQL query results
docs.text:
pyjelly reads and writes SPARQL query results in Jelly-SPARQL: the results of SELECT queries (solution sequences) and ASK queries (boolean results). Like Jelly-RDF, it is a compact binary format that can be written and read as a stream.

The media type of Jelly-SPARQL is application/x-jelly-sparql, and the file extension is .jellys.

docs.title: Usage with RDFLib
docs.text:
With pyjelly installed, RDFLib reads and writes query results in the jelly format, like it does json or xml:

from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.query import Result

graph = Graph()
graph.parse(
    data="""
        @prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
        <http://example.org/alice> foaf:name "Alice" ; foaf:knows <http://example.org/bob> .
        <http://example.org/bob> foaf:name "Bob" .
    """,
    format="turtle",
)

# Run a query and write its results in Jelly-SPARQL
results = graph.query("""
    PREFIX foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/>
    SELECT ?person ?name WHERE { ?person foaf:name ?name }
""")
results.serialize(destination="results.jellys", format="jelly")

# Read them back
with open("results.jellys", "rb") as file:
    parsed = Result.parse(file, format="jelly")

for row in parsed:
    print(f"{row.person} is called {row.name}")

# Results of ASK queries work the same way
answer = graph.query("ASK { ?person ?p 'Alice' }")
answer.serialize(destination="answer.jellys", format="jelly")
with open("answer.jellys", "rb") as file:
    print("Is anyone called Alice?", Result.parse(file, format="jelly").askAnswer)

Result.parse returns a JellySparqlResult (from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.sparql), which is an RDFLib Result with more attributes:

  • truncated – True if the stream ended without indicating that the results are complete. pyjelly also issues a JellyTruncatedResultsWarning then. A stream cut in the middle of a frame can't be read at all, and raises JellyConformanceError.
  • error – why the results are incomplete, in a sequence of results. See: incomplete results.
  • links – the IRIs of links that describe the results, like head.link in SPARQL JSON results.

RDFLib does not support RDF 1.2 yet, so triple terms and literals with a base direction can be read only with the generic API.

docs.title: Querying a SPARQL endpoint
docs.text:
RDFLib's SPARQLStore can ask a SPARQL endpoint for Jelly-SPARQL, if the endpoint offers it (e.g., Apache Jena Fuseki with the Jelly-JVM plugin):

from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.plugins.stores.sparqlstore import SPARQLStore

store = SPARQLStore(
    "http://localhost:3030/dataset/sparql",
    returnFormat="application/x-jelly-sparql",
)
for row in Graph(store=store).query("SELECT * WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } LIMIT 10"):
    print(row)

Warning

Use the media type, application/x-jelly-sparql, as returnFormat, not jelly.

docs.title: Large results
docs.text:
By default, Result.parse reads all rows at once. With Result.parse(file, format="jelly", lazy=True), the rows are read as the result is iterated, like RDFLib does with the results of its own queries. The stream must then stay open until you are done with the result.

When writing, the rows of an RDFLib result are written as the query makes them, so the first frames are written before the query is done. Each frame is flushed when it's written.

from rdflib import Literal, URIRef, Variable
from rdflib.query import Result

from pyjelly.errors import JellyIncompleteResultsError

# Many results, made one by one
results = Result("SELECT")
results.vars = [Variable("item"), Variable("number")]
results.bindings = (
    {
        Variable("item"): URIRef(f"http://example.org/item/{i}"),
        Variable("number"): Literal(i),
    }
    for i in range(100_000)
)
results.serialize(destination="many_results.jellys", format="jelly")

# Read the rows as they are needed, not all at once
with open("many_results.jellys", "rb") as file:
    parsed = Result.parse(file, format="jelly", lazy=True)
    try:
        total = sum(row.number.toPython() for row in parsed)
    except JellyIncompleteResultsError as error:
        # The writer said that the results are incomplete, e.g., the query failed
        print(f"Some results are missing: {error.error}")
        raise

print(f"The sum of the numbers is {total}")

Note

Iterate a lazy result with a for loop. list(result), len(result) and bool(result) read all of its rows first, as for any RDFLib result.

docs.title: Incomplete results
docs.text:
A query can fail after some of its results were already written, for example in case of a timeout, or a broken backend. Jelly-SPARQL then ends the stream with an error, so that readers know that the results are incomplete. pyjelly does this for you: if getting a row fails while results are being written, the stream ends with the error, and the error is raised.

When reading such results, pyjelly raises JellyIncompleteResultsError after the rows that were read. Its error attribute is the message of the writer, and its result attribute contains the results read before the error:

from pyjelly.errors import JellyIncompleteResultsError

try:
    result = Result.parse(file, format="jelly")
except JellyIncompleteResultsError as error:
    print(f"The query failed: {error.error}")
    partial_result = error.result

If you write results that you read from Jelly-SPARQL, and they were incomplete or truncated, pyjelly writes them as incomplete too.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
To change how results are written, pass SparqlOptions to serialize:

from pyjelly.options import LookupPreset, SparqlOptions

options = SparqlOptions(
    # Sizes of the lookups, see below
    lookup_preset=LookupPreset(max_names=4096, max_prefixes=256, max_datatypes=32),
    # How many values (rows times variables) a frame may have, at most
    frame_values=1024,
)
results.serialize(destination="results.jellys", format="jelly", options=options)

The default lookup sizes are 8192 names, 1024 prefixes and 64 datatypes, and a frame has at most 4096 values by default. Readers accept lookups of up to 16384 names, 4096 prefixes and 256 datatypes.

Note

LookupPreset() without arguments has the smaller defaults of Jelly-RDF (4000 names, 150 prefixes and 32 datatypes), not the defaults of SparqlOptions. Give all three sizes when you make a LookupPreset for SPARQL results.

With delimited=False, the results are written as one frame without its size, e.g., to be used in Kafka or MQTT. Then the lookups must be large enough to store all terms of the result set. Files and HTTP responses must be delimited, which is the default. To send the frames of the results as separate messages, see writing frame by frame.

docs.title: Sequences of results
docs.text:
A Jelly-SPARQL stream can also contain a sequence of results, e.g., the answers to a stream of queries, or to a query evaluated again and again. This is the PUNCTUATED stream type of Jelly-SPARQL. To write and read such a stream, use the functions in pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.sparql:

from pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.sparql import (
    parse_jelly_sparql_sequence,
    serialize_jelly_sparql_sequence,
)

with open("answers.jellys", "wb") as file:
    serialize_jelly_sparql_sequence([result_1, result_2, ask_result], file)

with open("answers.jellys", "rb") as file:
    for result in parse_jelly_sparql_sequence(file):
        print(result.type, len(result))

The lookups are shared by the results of the stream, so the terms they have in common are written once.

An incomplete result doesn't end a sequence, as there may be more results after it. parse_jelly_sparql_sequence doesn't raise an error for it, but sets its error attribute, so check it.

docs.title: Generic API
docs.text:
The generic API supports all of RDF 1.2. A row is a tuple with one value per variable, or None if the variable is unbound:

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.generic_sink import IRI, Literal
from pyjelly.integrations.generic.sparql import (
    parse_jelly_sparql,
    serialize_jelly_sparql,
)

alice = IRI("http://example.org/alice")
bob = IRI("http://example.org/bob")

# The rows of the results: one value per variable, None if it is unbound
rows = [
    (alice, Literal("Alice"), bob),
    (bob, Literal("Bob"), None),
]
with open("results.jellys", "wb") as file:
    serialize_jelly_sparql(["person", "name", "knows"], rows, file)

with open("results.jellys", "rb") as file:
    results = parse_jelly_sparql(file)
    print("Variables:", results.variables)
    # The rows are read as they are iterated, so before the file is closed
    for person, name, knows in results:
        print(person, name, knows)

parse_jelly_sparql returns a SparqlResultSet. Its rows are read as you iterate it, so the input must stay open until then, and the rows can be iterated only once. If the results are incomplete, iterating the rows raises JellyIncompleteResultsError after the last row.

serialize_jelly_sparql_ask writes the result of an ASK query. parse_jelly_sparql_sequence and serialize_jelly_sparql_sequence read and write sequences of results.

docs.title: Writing frame by frame
docs.text:
To write results frame by frame, e.g., to send each frame as a message over Kafka, use SparqlStream directly. It works with the terms of RDFLib (pyjelly.integrations.rdflib.sparql.sparql_stream()) or of the generic API (pyjelly.integrations.generic.sparql.sparql_stream()):

from pyjelly.integrations.generic.sparql import sparql_stream

stream = sparql_stream()
stream.start(["person", "name"])
for row in rows:
    # A frame, when it is full
    if frame := stream.row(row):
        send(frame.SerializeToString())
# The last frame of the results, which says they are complete
send(stream.end().SerializeToString())

If the results can't be completed, end them with stream.end("why") instead.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text: pyjelly passes the conformance tests of Jelly-SPARQL, with the generic API. The RDFLib integration passes all tests except those that use RDF 1.2 terms.

docs.title: Contributing to pyjelly
docs.text: Hi! This guide explains how to get started with developing pyjelly and contributing to it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
System requirements: while pyjelly works on any system that supports Python, for development we recommend using Linux, macOS, or WSL on Windows. We advise against using Windows directly, as it has caused many headaches in the past.

Clone the project: 

git clone --recursive git@github.com:Jelly-RDF/pyjelly.git

We use uv for package management. If you don't already have it, install uv.

On Linux this is: 

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Install the project:

uv sync

Note

If you use an IDE, make sure that it uses the Python interpreter from the environment that will be created in the .venv directory.

If you get an error about the uv version being incorrect, run uv self update

Activate the environment or use uv run to run commands and code.

docs.title: Giving feedback
docs.text:
The best way to send feedback is to file an issue at https://github.com/Jelly-RDF/pyjelly/issues

If you are proposing a feature:

  1. Explain how it would work.
  2. Keep the scope as narrow as possible, to make it easier to implement.
  3. Contributions are always welcome! Consider if you can help with implementing the feature.

docs.title: Contributing code
docs.text:
If you've found a major issue (not just a typo) or have a feature request, please open an issue first. This helps us keep track of what needs to be done and allows others to contribute as well.

When opening a pull request:

  • Use a descriptive title.
  • Clearly describe what the pull request does and why it is needed.
  • Reference the related issue in the description.

The CI will check if your code passes all checks. You can run these checks locally:

  • Tests: uv run pytest
  • Type safety: uv run mypy .
  • Linter: uv run ruff check --fix
  • Formatter: uv run ruff format

This helps us follow best practices and keep the codebase in shape.

docs.title: Contributing documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is written in Markdown and built using MkDocs, using Material for MkDocs.

To edit a documentation page, simply click the button in the top-right of the page.

It will take you to GitHub, where you can edit the Markdown file and submit a pull request. You can also clone the repository and edit the files locally. The source files are in the docs directory.

docs.title: Previewing documentation locally
docs.text:
Install dependencies for docs:

uv sync --group docs

Then, start a local docs server:

uv run mkdocs serve

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• More information on editing Jelly docs
  • Material for MkDocs reference
  • MkDocs documentation
  • Macro plugin documentation

docs.title: Making releases
docs.text:
1. Make sure you are on the main branch and that it is up-to-date: git checkout main && git pull.
  2. Create a new tag for the release. For example, for version 1.2.3: git tag v1.2.3. The tag must start with v!
  3. Push the tag to GitHub: git push origin v1.2.3.
  4. The release will be automatically built and published to PyPI.

docs.title: Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct
docs.text: This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html.

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

docs.title: Our Standards
docs.text:
Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

  • Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
  • Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
  • Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
  • Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

docs.title: Enforcement Responsibilities
docs.text:
Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official email address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at community@neverblink.eu. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

docs.title: Enforcement Guidelines
docs.text: Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

docs.title: 1. Correction
docs.text:
Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

docs.title: 2. Warning
docs.text:
Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

docs.title: 3. Temporary Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

docs.title: 4. Permanent Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder.

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations.
